steps.say: Many childhood neck lumps are leftover developmental tracts, not swollen glands. They can appear as cysts, open channels, cartilage nubs, pits or skin tags, often leaking clear sticky fluid.
steps.tx: Not every childhood neck lump is a node. **Branchial cleft** (gill arch leftover) remnants form lateral neck masses when arches, clefts and pouches fail to regress. They appear as cysts, sinuses, a **fistula** (open tract), **cartilaginous rests** (firm cartilage nubs), dermal pits or skin tags, often with **mucoid drainage** (clear sticky discharge). A pit or tag at birth marks the tract, so examine every newborn neck lump for a tiny skin opening.

steps.say: The commonest remnant sits at a classic spot on the big strap muscle of the neck. A discharging pit at the junction of its upper half and lower third is a second cleft remnant until proven otherwise.
steps.tx: The commonest remnant has a classic address. **Second branchial cleft** (second arch leftover) anomalies are the most frequent type. The **external ostium** (skin opening) sits along the anterior border of the **sternocleidomastoid** (strap neck muscle), usually at the junction of its upper half and lower third. A discharging pit there in a child is a second cleft remnant until proven otherwise, and infection makes the tract swell, redden and ache.

rows: SCM junction, upper and lower third
In front of or behind the ear

steps.say: The second cleft channel runs a deep course past the great vessels and two cranial nerves to the tonsil bed. Follow the whole road at surgery, because nerves and vessels hug the tract.
steps.tx: The second cleft tract follows a deep road every surgeon must know. The fistula rises along the carotid sheath to the hyoid, turns medially to pass between the limbs of the **carotid bifurcation** (carotid fork), then runs past the **hypoglossal nerve** (tongue nerve) and the glossopharyngeal nerve behind the digastric muscle to end in the **tonsillar fossa** (tonsil bed). Dissection must trace this whole path, since nerves and vessels hug the tract wall.

steps.say: A long twisting channel cannot be delivered through a single cut. Open stepwise counter cuts higher in the neck, and never yank the tract, because a remnant guarantees return and blind pulling endangers vessels and nerves.
steps.tx: A long twisting tract cannot come out through one cut. Long tortuous fistulas need **stepladder incision** (stepwise counter cuts) for **complete excision** (whole tract removal), opening a second or third small incision higher in the neck to deliver the upper tract. Any leftover **fistula tract** (remaining channel) guarantees recurrence, and blind pulling risks the carotid, the jugular and nearby nerves, so the tract is dissected, never yanked.

steps.say: Lumps around the ear play by different rules, because their channel runs through the salivary gland beside the face movement nerve. Always find that nerve first before removing anything here.
steps.tx: Lumps around the ear follow different rules. **First branchial cleft** (first arch leftover) anomalies sit in front of or behind the ear, or in the upper neck near the mandible. Their fistulas course through the parotid gland, passing through or around **facial nerve** (face movement nerve) branches to reach the **external auditory canal** (ear channel). Every excision here starts by identifying the facial nerve, since an unmapped tract can divide it and palsy the face.

steps.say: Low neck lumps in toddlers can dive toward the chest, so map the lower end with scans before any cut. Firm cartilage containing cysts near the collarbone belong to the third cleft family.
steps.tx: Low neck lumps in toddlers hide a deeper threat. **Third branchial cleft** (third pouch leftover) remnants sit at the **suprasternal notch** (neck base dip) or the clavicle and can descend into the **mediastinum** (chest centre). They present as firm cysts or abscesses in toddlers and often contain cartilage. Because the tract dives toward the chest, imaging must map its lower end before any cut, and chest surgeons may need to join the case.

steps.say: Hard painless growing nodes above the collarbone with fevers at night and weight loss warn of cancer. Scan the chest for hidden nodes, while small tender nodes on both sides of a passing cold simply need watching.
steps.tx: Some neck nodes warn of cancer, not infection. A fixed nontender enlarging **supraclavicular node** (collarbone node) with night sweats and weight loss raises **malignancy** (cancer) concern and needs chest imaging to hunt **mediastinal adenopathy** (chest nodes). In contrast, acute bilateral small tender nodes from a viral cold need observation alone, without biopsy or antibiotics, since they melt away as the cold passes.

steps.say: Ordinary bacterial nodes settle with antibiotics, but purple fluctuant nodes from atypical mycobacteria do not. Those need the whole node cut out, because medicines alone fail and a simple cut leaves a permanently draining hole.
steps.tx: Bacterial nodes and mycobacterial nodes behave differently. **Staphylococcus aureus** (staph germ) and group A streptococcus cause most acute **pyogenic lymphadenitis** (pus forming node infection), which responds to antibiotics with drainage when fluctuant. Fluctuant violaceous nodes instead suggest **nontuberculous mycobacteria** (atypical TB germs) needing **surgical excision** (cutting the node out), because these germs resist chemotherapy and a simple incision forms a chronic draining sinus.
